questions.title: Why does the block-diagonal structure in OFT limit expressiveness of the orthogonal matrix?
questions.question_body: In Section 3, the authors mention that a block-diagonal orthogonal matrix cannot approximate classic linear transforms, whereas a dense orthogonal matrix can. I understand that a block-diagonal structure partitions the neuron dimensions into independent groups, but I’m unclear on why this fundamentally prevents us from approximating transforms like the discrete Fourier transform or a full random orthogonal matrix. Could someone provide an intuitive explanation or a small example demonstrating this limitation?

questions.title: How does the information transmission framework translate a butterfly factorisation into a sparse graph?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces an ‘information transmission view’ where an orthogonal matrix $ m{R}$ is seen as transmitting information over a $d	imes(m+1)$ grid graph. I’m struggling to connect this view to the concrete butterfly factorisation $	ilde{ m{B}}(d,2^k)$. Specifically, how does a butterfly matrix correspond to directed edges in this grid, and how many edges are required to guarantee dense connectivity? A diagram or explicit mapping would help.

questions.title: What guarantees that each butterfly component $	ilde{ m{B}}(d,k)$ can be rendered orthogonal?
questions.question_body: Equation (4) defines a butterfly component as a block‑diagonal matrix of $k	imes k$ butterflies, and later the authors say each component can be parameterized as an orthogonal matrix using Cayley transform or $2$‑dimensional rotations. However, for $k>2$ the blocks are not just simple rotations; they involve multiple diagonal sub‑blocks. How exactly do we ensure that the whole $	ilde{ m{B}}(d,k)$ is orthogonal? Is there a closed‑form condition on the vectors $ m{d}_i$ that guarantees orthogonality for all $k$?

questions.title: Why does BOFT(	extit{m},	extit{b}) reduce parameters from $ oldsymbol{O}(d^2)$ to $ oldsymbol{O}(d oldsymbol{	extit{m}})$?
questions.question_body: The paper states that BOFT with parameters $(m,b)$ has 	frac12(b-1)dm effective trainable parameters for a layer of size $d	imes n$, leading to $O(d oldsymbol m)$ when $b=2$. Could someone walk through the counting argument? In particular, how many free parameters do we have in each $2b	imes 2b$ block of a butterfly component, and how does this sum over all components?

questions.title: How is multiplicative dropout implemented in BOFT compared to standard dropout?
questions.question_body: Section 5.1 describes ‘multiplicative dropout’ for BOFT: randomly picking some butterfly components and diagonal blocks and replacing them with identity matrices. How does this differ mathematically from applying standard dropout on the weight updates? Would it be equivalent to zeroing out certain entries, or is it conceptually different because of the multiplicative update rule?

questions.title: Can BOFT approximate any arbitrary orthogonal matrix with sufficiently many layers?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 claims that by composing enough butterfly matrices we can span the whole orthogonal group. Yet earlier in Section 4 it was argued that BOFT has limited expressiveness compared to full OFT. Are these statements contradictory? Under what conditions (values of $m$, $b$, or additional steps) does BOFT become universal? Is there an intuitive way to see why increasing $m$ alone doesn’t guarantee universality?

questions.title: Is preserving spectral norm necessary for training stability in finetuning?
questions.question_body: "Spectral properties" mentions that multiplying by an orthogonal matrix preserves the spectral norm of $ m{W}^0$, aiding stability. Could someone elaborate on why this preservation is beneficial? Does it prevent gradient explosion/saturation more effectively than other methods (e.g., LayerNorm)? Is there empirical evidence showing training diverges without spectral preservation?

questions.title: "Information transmission" vs. classic fast linear transform!
questions.question_body: "BOFT uses sparse multiplication like a network topology” – I’d like to understand when BOFT’s butterfly factorisation actually mimics classical fast transforms such as FFT or Hadamard. Are there settings of $ m d_i$ that recover those transforms exactly? If so, how is this special case reflected in the training objective?

questions.title: "Injective inductive bias" – what does it mean for BF's sparse factorization?
questions.question_body: "Inductive bias and generalization in BOFT” says that sparse factorization may induce an implicit inductive bias similar to other sparse training works. What theoretical intuition or prior results support this claim? How might such bias manifest in practice (e.g., encouraging certain invariances)?
